utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated and have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the Judges would like to have a closed session before the witness comes in, or private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Mrs. Papic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're not going to remain standing for very long, let me tell you that right away. First of all, give us your name, your given name, your place and date of birth and where you're currently residing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Poculica. I'm staying in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You were born in Poculica, if I'm not mistaken. How old are you? What is your date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in '39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing for a few more moments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in '39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you remember the date and the month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The 3rd of which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In March, in 1939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The 3rd of March. Thank you. Yes, it was in March. And what was the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 13th. The 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It was the 13th of March. Thank you very much. I'm saying this for the Defence: Mrs. Mara Papic was born on the 13th of March, 1939. Please read the oath, but perhaps if you have difficulties reading, the registrar will read it for you. The registrar will read to you a statement -- a declaration, rather, and you will nod your approval of that declaration. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If would you repeat after me. "I solemnly declare."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "That I will speak the truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "The whole truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "And nothing but truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Papic, you may be seated now. Relax, Mrs. Papic, you have nothing to fear. You have agreed to come to a far away country, in respect of your own country. Do not be afraid. If you're tired, tell us that you're tired. You're going to answer questions that will first be asked by the counsel working for General Blaskic, and then you will be asked questions by the Office of the Prosecutor, and the Judges may also ask you some questions. Don't be afraid. You are accused of nothing, but you are the one who is coming to testify, and we are appreciative of that. Do you feel all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I think that we can begin now. Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Papic, just a few more things about you. You said that you were born on the 13th of March, 1939 in Poculica. Did you live in Poculica until the war with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Now I live in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a displaced person?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you return to your house?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I have three, two daughters and one son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're a widow.

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, did you ever appear before a court of law? Did you ever go to prison? Were you ever punished in such a way in your life?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No, I've never been to a court of law in my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never. So this is the first time?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could we have a map distributed? There's original and copies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D449.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we start, before you start making your statement, could you please explain to the Court whether it is correct that you and I made up this map? You showed me the direction in which you were fleeing from Poculica, and then I pasted this red arrow on the map, and the circle shows Poculica, your village, and Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until the war broke out you lived in Poculica. Tell us, did Muslims and Croats live together in Poculica?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes. The mosque was right over here, and then there were the Croats and then over here were the Muslims, and the Croats. From my house, down there, there were more Croats. It wasn't that mixed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get along with your Muslim neighbours? Could you please describe that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Very nicely. Very nicely. When it was Bajram we would go to see them, and when we celebrated Christmas they came to see us. I have a neighbour, there's only a fence between our yard and their yard. And, you know, we were all retired persons and we weren't exactly well-off, and whatever was ours was theirs and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything frighten you on Easter when you saw some men with long beards who were practising something? Was it your neighbours, your Muslim neighbours who frightened you in any way? Please describe what you saw.

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, they were walking down the road, and these people were running along exercising, doing something, you know, a long beard, a long -- and long blonde hair too, and I never saw that before. Nobody in our parts wears a long beard and long hair like that. I asked my neighbour, Smajo, "What is this? Why are these people running down" --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And your neighbour is a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He's called Smajo. So I asked him, and he said, "Well, these are foreigners. These are Mujahedin. They've come to our place to Prnjavor, don't be frightened." We never thought that something would come out of it, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please tell the Court, on the 15th of April, 1993, that is a day before the shooting actually broke out in your village, what were you doing? Did you notice that there would be a war? Did you go to a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes. We went to a meeting, and the municipality of Vitez convened all of us to a meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you mean "all of us"? Who was all of you?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: All of us, the Muslims and the Croats. We were retirees and they wanted to give us something. We spent about an hour at this meeting, and we went home and we don't know a thing after that. This neighbour of mine, he walked me home and -- we walked together, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the municipality of Vitez wish to give seed to both you and the Muslims so that you could actually do your agricultural work in the spring, right, so you could plant whatever you had to?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it given to both of you?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was given to both of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Muslims and the Croats. We did it together, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day, the 16th of April, 1993, before the shooting started in your village, who called you and who told you what? And how many minutes before that?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: About ten minutes before all that my sister phoned me, and she said, "Hey, have you heard all this shooting?" I said, "No, no, I can't hear any shooting. Where?" She said to me, "Go up there to momma's." You know, our mother lives near the school, between the Muslims and the Croats. She said, "Go and get our mother." Our mother is old. She's 80 years old. I went to get my mother, and I called my son to go to Grebenar. I mean, that was the commander if --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute. Sorry. We have to wait a little bit to have your words translated, so we're going to make small pauses as we speak. Where was your son at daybreak? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: They were on guard duty together, the Muslims and the Croats. They were walking up and down the road. I don't know. Some kind of guard duty because of these Serbian -- I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, your son, did he know that there would be a war?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. When I said, "Go over there to Grebenar," we could hear shooting, my sister called me, "Let's see what's going to happen, what we're going to do." And that's when it started shooting all over the place, when Grebenar came to my house, he made a phone call to Vitez and they said, "We don't know a thing." And they said, "Yes, there's shooting some place but we don't know either."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, Grebenar was the commander in your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander, and he came to my place straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Grebenar made this phone call to Vitez and that they -- when they said that they also saw that there was shooting but they didn't know exactly where, what happened in your village? Was there shelling or what?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: There was shooting all over the place. Behind the mosque where the Croatian houses were, there was shooting there, and they took our Croat people and they drove them away from the mosque. They took them to prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, did shells start falling around your house and in this Croatian part of the village?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: First the sheds were on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose sheds?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: And right by the mosque, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that person a Croat?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he's a Croat, and his shed and Kristo Bozo's shed and his stable also caught fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he also Croat?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is also a Croat. Ten minutes later, Stipan Ramnjak's two houses and stable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He is also a Croat?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is. Then all these Croat houses below my house -- I mean, that was the Croatian part of the village, and then shells started falling all over it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your house is closer to the Muslim houses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the shells started to fall on the Croatian houses, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: We were in my basement, about 28 of us, women and children. When a shell fell on my stable, then the women and children were wondering where to go. There are some bushes leading from my house to the brook, and we realised that we had to run away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we actually describe how you ran away, tell me, is it correct that the stables of Frano Jurcevic and Kristo Bozo, Croats, burned down around 9.00?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Anto was also wounded near his house, by the shed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, he's a civilian. He's 65 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that around 10.00 two houses and the shed of Stipan Ramnjak, also a Croat, were burned down?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any resistance by Croatian soldiers in Poculica then?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I couldn't get out of the basement. Only when I really had to get something from upstairs, then I would race out. I saw smoke, and I saw these houses and stables and sheds on fire, then I would run back into the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, at 11.00 what happened to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: You know, we have these loud speakers, and when the Hodza is up there and then his prayer resounds throughout the village, you know, how they pray to God, and they were shouting from the top of the mosque, "Croats, surrender your arms. If you don't surrender your arms we're going to kill each and every one of you wherever we find you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Grebenar again? What did he tell you? What were you supposed to do? What was he going to do? Would he negotiate?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: We started running away. We got down there to the brook, and -- and they were shouting that they would slaughter us. And we panicked, and we run down to the brook, and I saw Grebenar down there and he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that, the Muslims who were assembled around the mosque, did they send Vlado Ramnjak, a Croat to you?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: He went down the road, and they told him to go down to Grebenar. "Why doesn't Grebenar come to negotiate?" And they said, "If you come back we are going to kill your wife, and your two children and also your disabled brother," who was in a wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Vlado Ramnjak then?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Grebenar and Vlado were standing there, and Grebenar was wounded because a shell fell, and Vlado had to go up to -- back to his wife and children in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the shell fall as they were negotiating, Vlado Ramnjak, who was sent by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Commander Grebenar? Did the shell fall at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm sure it did fall as soon as Vlado ran away and the other one went down to the brook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About 3.00 p.m., did you see some men, wearing black, going down from the mosque, coming down from the mosque?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I went out to take my documents from the upper floor and take them down to the basement if we had to flee, to have my documents with me. I saw about 150 metres towards the school, everything was black. Lots of people wearing black uniforms, and they had rifles, and they had some sort of scarves, and they were coming towards us and we had to flee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you flee in the direction of that red arrow down by the brook, towards Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes. There's a stream below my house and we went downstream to Krizancevo Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, how many civilians fled and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Well, about 80 children -- about 100 perhaps. There were lots of children as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to you when you were fleeing downstream? Were you shelled? Did they shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: There was shelling all over the place, and one shell fell by my barn, by my shed, and I took up a child, a 17-month-old child, and its mother took up her -- one of her children who was of school age and a second child who was three years old, and we were down by the stream when the shells began to fall. They fell everywhere. I looked up, I raised my head to see where a shell would be falling, and I fell down, and the child that I was carrying fell down and it broke its arm. It was all I could do to get to Krizancevo Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the feeling that they were shooting at you civilians who were trying to flee by the stream?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was shelling at us. They would -- the shells would fall in front us or behind us as we were escaping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, did you hear them taking prisoners from your village, and did you hear that they were taken away?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: When we got to Krizancevo Selo, and when we said, "Where's this man and where's the other man," and they would tell us they had all been arrested and taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Krizancevo Selo, where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd I went to Vitez. A Serb gave me an apartment. He worked with my son, and he called my son to come to his apartment, that he would give up his apartment and take him in, give him accommodation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Dubravica, Krizancevo Selo, Vitez, all these places, which are very near, did you and the other people talk about what had happened? Did you tell the citizens there how the Muslims attacked you?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did tell these stories but nobody believed me until they had seen the child with the broken arm, and his arm was put in plaster, and then they began to believe us, that they had been, in fact, shooting at us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, please, something about the Croat houses, the Croat houses in Poculica. What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: They were all set fire to and they were shelled. Everything was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in your own house -- did you visit your own house after these events?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, a month and a half ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you find in your house?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: There's an Askic living there, and Sljivcica and his wife. When I went into my house and said, "Good morning," she said, "Good morning," and I said, "I've just come to see what there is left in my house." She said to me, "There's nothing belonging to you here. Everything has been destroyed. There's nothing." I just said, "I know that everything in the house belongs to me. You are sleeping on my couch. That belongs to me." And when I went on the 11th for the Sesvete celebration, there was nothing in the house, just one couch and one stove. Everything had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anybody else living in your house?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Just this man and a woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's a number from Donja Veceriska. His name is Askic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're a widow. Did you go to pay your respects to your husband at the cemetery? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Well, when the cease-fire was signed we went to the cemetery. Which is located in the Muslim village. Our cemetery is up above, at a height. When we went to the cemetery there was, no tombstones were standing. They had all been knocked down, the chapel had been knocked down, the fence had been destroyed. It was a terrible sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you rebuild something in the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Well, one month later we went back to the cemetery to try and repair the fence and cover the chapel, and we just lined up the tombstones. The stones that had fallen, we set them right. We found that everything had been shelled, little bits and pieces were shattered all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have finished. We would like to tender in evidence this map which shows Poculica, the arrow showing the direction in which the people fled, and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Papic, you're going to be asked some questions by the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, that's a normal procedure. I'm sure they explained this to you. Mr. Harmon. Cross-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Papic, my name is Mark Harmon. I'm with the Prosecutor's office. To my right is Mr. Andrew Cayley, and to his right is Mr. Gregory Kehoe. I'm going to ask you just a few questions. First of all, Mrs. Papic, could you describe for me, in a little more detail, your village. I understand it was a mixed village with Croats and Muslims living in the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people lived in your village?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: About 100, with their families, altogether. About 100 people altogether. Men, and women and so forth. There were not many of us Croats, about a hundred, with their families, together with the families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the 100 families, was that 100 Croat and Muslim families or was that just 100 Croat families?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: One hundred Croat families. Prnjavor and Poculica, that was together. Vrhovine, that was in Poculica. That was much -- they were much bigger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you had a Muslim neighbour that you told us about by the name of Smajo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right. We were divided by a fence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the Croat population in the village of Poculica one that was mixed together with the Muslim population or were the two ethnic groups segregated in distinct parts of the village?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No, they were all together, Prnjavor, Vrhovine and Poculica, all together, and Poculica. And the Croat village was just from my house down there, there were about 50 houses, 50 Croat houses. From my house, up above they were Croats and Muslims. So there would be one Croat house, one Muslim house, one Croat house, one Muslim house, or across the road there would be the Muslims there, and this side the Croats. And this was how it was right up to the mosque. Up by the mosque there was a fence again which separated the Croats by the mosque. The road went towards the mosque and this is where the Croats were, the mosque was here. And then, once again, there were Muslims further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what I understand from your testimony, Mrs. Papic, in some areas the Croats and the Muslims were mixed together, and in some areas of Poculica the Muslims lived separately in their own ethnic group, and in --

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me finish. And in some areas the Croats had a distinct and definable area where they lived separately; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, they all lived together, it was just that they were up by the mosque, both the Croats and the Muslims, up by the mosque. Whereas down below, from my house going lower were the Croat houses, but we were all together. And the municipality was the municipality of Prnjavor, that was our municipality, and it was a Muslim local community, Croats and Muslims alike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Papic, in terms of area, in terms of size of the village of Poculica, was it a big village or was it a very small village?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Well, a sort of medium size village, not a very big village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it cover much area? Was it spread out? Were the houses and residences concentrated together in what may be a village centre?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Well, fences. Here you have the road, then the Muslim houses, then the Croat houses. It was all very near, nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Divided by these fences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to the morning of the 16th of April, and you testified that you received a phone call from your sister who called you and asked you if you had heard any shooting, and your testimony was that you answered, "No, I haven't heard any shooting." Did I understand your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I heard shooting, but I didn't know where the shooting was taking place, but I just heard it. Then I went up to fetch my mother and bring her down to us, because she lived alone in her own house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go fetch your mother, or did one of your relatives, one of your children go get your mother?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No, I went to get my mother. She wasn't far off, she was 50 metres away from me. I went to get my mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately what time was that on the morning of the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I don't know, I can't give you the exact time, I didn't look at clock. I can't really tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, once you and your mother returned to your house, did you and the other people in your neighbourhood go down into your basement?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were 28 of us with the children that we had taken in from across the road when it started, when the shooting started. I called out to these women and I said, "Come down to my basement," because Smajo was close by and all of his family were all close together. So I called out to the them and said, "Let's take cover in my basement, because I have a good basement."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you went into your basement sometime in the morning hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, it was morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you remain in your basement until approximately 3.00 in the afternoon when you left your house?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were in the basement all the time. But I just had to go from the basement up into the upper floor, and I was able to see Poculica burn, and the shelling, and I had to flee to avoid being hit. But when my barn was hit, well, then, that was a real commotion and we decided to flee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mrs. Papic, while you were in your house, you went upstairs at least on one occasion, did you leave the basement on more than one occasion to look outside and see what was happening in your village? Or was it only on one occasion that you did that?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I went five or six times, I had to go upstairs because everything was upstairs. I had my larder upstairs, and I had to give, go and get food for the children and give the children some food to eat down below. They -- I had to give the children milk, so I had to look for the bottles in the floor upstairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you would go upstairs, would you conduct your particular searches for the milk and searches for the food, would you do that quickly and then return to the basement quickly in order to avoid being hurt?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Quite certainly, because there was shelling, so you have to flee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it I'm correct, Mrs. Papic, you were never in the military and have no experience in military matters, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. I'm a housewife. I've got nothing to do with all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you, while you were in your house on the 16th of April, and in the basement for the majority of the time, were you able to determine where the shells that were being fired on the village of Poculica were coming from?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Tolovici were over here, and they were Muslims. Here we have Vrhovine and Prnjavor, once again Muslim. Sljivcica was over there, Muslims, again, only Muslims, Muslim inhabitants. And Vjetrenice behind us, and it came from all sides. So when a shell is being launched, you can't see exactly where it's coming from. But when we were in the stream, in the brook, from Sljivcica we could hear shots coming from Sljivcica, and then the shell would fall in the stream where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Papic, I will come to the time when you were in the stream in a few minutes in my questions. But while you were in the house in your basement, were you able to determine where the shells were coming from?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I would go out and hear it coming from Sljivcica, from up above towards the Croat village on the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mrs. Papic, that on the morning of the 16th HVO forces were shelling the village of Poculica from the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No. A shell cannot come from Vitez, it can come from Sljivcica, Sljivcica is nearer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that the HVO was shelling the village of Poculica on the morning of the 16th with a 40 millimetre anti-aircraft gun and a six barrel multi-rocket launcher from Gradina?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that on the 18th of April the HVO was shelling the village of Poculica?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think you already asked that question, Mr. Harmon. The witness already answered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you left your basement you and the other people who had been in your basement fled down a creek and you went in the direction of Krizancevo Selo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Krizancevo Selo, Krizanac Krizancevo Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was on the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 16th of April, 1993, when was the first time that you returned to Poculica?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: We returned when the cease-fire had been signed. As soon as the cease-fire had been signed we went to the cemetery, to our cemetery. The cease-fire had been signed, and I didn't go after that until there was a mass said at the cemetery. That was one year later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say the cease-fire, are you talking about when the war between the Muslims and the Croats ended? Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's at that point in time when you saw some of the houses that had belonged to the Croats had been damaged or destroyed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I saw immediately when we began to flee. I saw this immediately, because it was a hill and you can see the Croats houses, and I could see the Croat houses burning down below as soon as we started to flee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any Muslim houses burning or any Muslim barns burning?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: They were higher up above. There was a plateau, there was a plain down below, so you could see this part while we were fleeing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you see the Muslim houses burning and the Muslim barns burning as well?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: They were up above, here, so you can't really. They are up above, so you can't really, so you're going down the slope and come to the Croat villages, and so you could see these when we were fleeing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in your village, when you left, Mrs. Papic, did you see any Muslim houses or barns on fire or damaged?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I couldn't have been there, as I've just told you. I couldn't have gone out to see this, because they were up above me; whereas, Asim and the others near me, that remained intact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was your house that you returned to a year later, was your house destroyed by some force, either shells or fire, or was it intact?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: The shed was destroyed, the doors were taken away, the bathroom had been destroyed, there was no water. That's it, when I went into the house, that's what I found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But your house was standing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, the house was standing, and the man went to live there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your immediate neighbourhood where you lived, Mrs. Papic, after you returned, after the cease-fire, were there other Croat houses that were still standing in your village?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There was my brother's house, two of them. This was a Muslim one, and up above a Croat house. Two brothers, Muslims, on this side, and all the houses were standing and people were living in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So not all the houses that belonged to the Croats in Poculica were damaged or destroyed as a result of the conflict on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No, no. Yes, not all of them. The upper part remained, the Croats and the Muslims, those houses, except for Stipan Ramnjak, his house burned down, both his houses and the barn. Only his house was burned between the Muslims and Croats. Whereas, from my house down the slope, which is only the Croat houses, those houses were shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you know somebody by the name of Redzo Bektas? Pardon my pronunciation. Is that a name that's familiar to you? Let me try pronouncing it again. Do you know a family by the name of Bektas?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No, we had a Bektas, but he is in Vitez, and he was in the local community in Prnjavor. But he went away a long time ago. So we had this municipality with the Croats and Muslims and that was that particular Bektas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Papic, you and your friends who were in the basement fled, but were there other Croats who remained in Poculica after the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Those who were in prison stayed, but those who could run, when they realised what was going on, there was shooting and they were shooting all over, everybody escaped down to the stream. And we got up to Krizancevo Selo at 6.00 only from the stream down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there were 28 people in your group who fled, and earlier in your testimony you said there were about 100 Croat families who lived in the village of Poculica.

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Twenty-eight women and children in my basement. Women and children in my basement, I did not say anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your testimony you said there were about 100 families, Croat families who lived in your village. Did some of those Croats from Poculica remain in Poculica after the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Those who were imprisoned. Half of them stayed on, and the other half fled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After they were released from prison, did they return to Poculica?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No, not a single one has returned to Poculica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Papic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, do you want to exercise your right of redirect? Do you have additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Two or three, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was thinking about the break, let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Nobilo, try to finish before the break Re-examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Papic, I would like to put two or three questions to you. Tell us, please, after the war broke out between the Muslims and the Croats, apart from those who were arrested, did a single Croat stay in Poculica?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Only those who were killed, I'm talking about Bozo Kristo, I don't know of anyone else who stayed on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those who were arrested, did they go back to Poculica or did they go back to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, after the exchange they came to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell us, Mrs. Papic, later on, when you came to Poculica, did you see a single Muslim house that had been set on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No, not a single one. Where we passed, not a single Muslim house had been set on fire or shelled, not a single shell had fallen on any one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, that day when the shelling took place and when you fled after that, did a single shell fall on Muslim houses, on the Muslim part of the village?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: They are up above me and I couldn't see up there. Because as I was running away, this is the way my house is, this is where the creek is, and from here, I could see our Croat houses over there, you know. And as I was running, I would turn around and I would see the smoke coming from the Croat houses down there, and I saw they were on fire and they had been shelled, and I saw these shells too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you hear any explosions around the Muslim part of the village, around the mosque? Were there explosions or not?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the purely Croatian part of the village was fully destroyed and in the mixed part of the village the Croat houses remained standing except for the two or three that you mentioned. Who lives in these Croat houses that were intact that are in the mixed part of the Poculica village?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: All of them are Muslims. My brother's two houses. All over it is Muslims living there now, and in my house there are Muslims living.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question. Please tell the Court whether a single Croat has returned to Poculica until this present day, now that you're testifying before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No, we weren't even told to come back, and they weren't asking us to come back, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad you had a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mrs. Papic. The Prosecutor, Mr. Mark Harmon, asked you if you knew if your village of Poculica was shelled from Vitez on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993, and it was also shelled from Gradina; do you know anything about that, about where the shelling came from? Did any people tell you, or are you just guessing where it came from?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Nobody told us, but it cannot reach from Vitez to Poculica. I mean, you cannot shell from Vitez. It's only from Tolovici that are nearby, and you can hear it, also, when it is fired from Tolovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So, you don't think the Prosecutor was right when he told you that the shelling was from Vitez and from Gradina, you refuse this?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Of course I refuse it. You can't, Sljivcica was nearer, so when they shoot from Sljivcica we can hear it in the basement. We know exactly that it is going to fall here. And where is Vitez? I mean, way out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Poculica was in a Muslim area, all the villages around it were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And how far was it from Vitez and from Gradina?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: That I don't know. You're asking me, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The villages around you, since the villages are close, were they also shelled; or was it just your village which was shelled?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I know that they were in Sljivcica and that they were shelling only Poculica. The Muslims were at Sljivcica, and then over there at Tolovici and Vrhovine, and they're nearby, and you can hear all of it coming from there, and you can hear and feel this fall on the Croatian houses in the Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The other villages around you which are close, were they also shelled, the other Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I don't know, you can't see that. When there's only hills around, you can't see the houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you didn't see anything around you?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: On the morning did you have breakfast?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No way. Nobody had a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: When your daughter rang you and asked you if you had heard any shooting, was that before or after the time when you would normally have breakfast?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: She woke me up, because I like to sleep late in the morning. I haven't got a thing to do, so I just sleep in late. And she woke me up saying, "Get up, can't you hear the shooting?" And as I got up, then I heard the shooting. And she told me to go to my mother's so my mother could stay with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Was it daylight or was it dark?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: It was daylight, 8.00, I think, I'm sure. It was daylight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: When you went to Vitez, can you tell us, what were the conditions there? Was anything very special going on in or around Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know, I didn't really pay any attention. I mean, I got this apartment, naturally, and I tried to settle in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You didn't see any shooting happening at Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I didn't, then, not then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're almost finished Mrs. Papic. Is your village far away from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, our village is far away from Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you heard about what happened in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: We didn't hear a thing then, when we were running away. We were in creeks and basements and we didn't hear a thing about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps not on that date, but later on, later on, did you hear about what had happened in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I didn't, I didn't go out. I didn't go anywhere. I was just trying to settle in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So you've never heard about Ahmici and about the massacres that took place there?

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any interest, you know. I didn't go out, I didn't have a TV set or a radio, nothing. I didn't have a thing when I became a refugee, and I couldn't find out anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have one last question. You really don't have to answer it. What made you come to testify in this trial of an accused that you don't really know? What was the reason that you came? If you don't want to answer that question, don't answer. I haven't heard your answer, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MARA PAPIC
utterances.text: No. I -- nothing really made me. I mean, I just wanted to say what had happened to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right. We thank you for having come here, for having taken such a long trip to tell us about what happened in your village. You're now going to be escorted out of the courtroom. The Judges are going to withdraw and we'll take a break until noon, and you can go home. I hope that you will find some peace when you get back. The Court stands adjourned. We will start again at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We'll now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness. The witness is Slavko Katava.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking for the summary. Here it is, the summary in French. Registrar, if you would give the English copies to my colleagues. All right. We'll have Mr. Slavko Katava brought in, who is not covered by protective measures. You don't have the date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have it and we've given it to the Prosecutor this morning, Mr. President, just a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's fine (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: -- of September, 1956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, please give us your name, your given names, your date and place of birth, your profession and your current residence. After that, you will take an oath and then you may be seated. All right. Mr. Katava, go ahead, please. We are listening to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my name is Slavko Katava. I was born in 1956 in Donja Polje, the municipality of Busovaca. I reside in Busovaca. I am a policeman by profession. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you will take your oath. You will read the oath in your own language, the oath which has been given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Katava, you may be seated. You're going to answer questions that you will be asked. You've agreed to participate in the trial of the -- trial of General Blaskic, who is in this courtroom. You will first -- I'm sure it's been explained to you, first answer Mr. Nobilo's questions. Is that right? Yes. Then you will be questioned by the Office of the Prosecutor, and the Judges' questions will complete your testimony. Mr. Nobilo, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, explain to the court, please, what schools you have completed and when.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I went to Hesa (phoen) Primary School in Busovaca. After that I went to the police school in Sarajevo, and I have been working in the police force since 1974. I worked in the police station of Teslic. I worked there up until 1977, when I was transferred to the police station in Busovaca where I work today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, you have been a policeman throughout your career?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Yes. Since I finished school I've been a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many years is that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: It is 26 years now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Starting out from the disintegration of Yugoslavia in 1991 and the first democratic elections, can you explain to the Trial Chamber what the organisation of the police force in Busovaca was like? First of all, within the frameworks of what Ministry, and what was the transformation that took place later on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: After the first democratic elections were held, the police force was headed by the party people, the people of the victorious party, and the police still functioned in the old setup, that is to say, as a police station for Busovaca with its security services in Zenica and the Internal Affairs Ministry at the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, can you tell us when the police force was reorganised, and when the police force was organised on -- in a new way in the -- and the police station in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: That time -- at the time it was obvious that the police force was not able to function as it had hitherto. There were divisions. The Muslims went to Muslim policemen, whereas the Croat population would contact the Croat police, and so the police department in Travnik was set up for an area covering the majority -- a majority Croat population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that your immediate superiors were the police department in Travnik. Can you tell us, at the police department in Travnik, what police stations belonged to the Travnik headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: The police stations of Fojnica, Kresevo, Kiseljak, Busovaca, Vitez, Novi Travnik, Travnik, Bugojno, Gorni Vakuf, and I think Jajce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this reorganisation coincide with the introduction of the HVO civilian authorities in Herceg-Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Yes, I think it coincided with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you and your police station are once again part of a united federal police force which includes Muslims and Croats alike; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We have a federal police force for the Central Bosnia region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go back to 1992/1993, how were the appointments made? Who appointed, for example, the commander, the Chief of Police? Who determined who this would be; who would be a policeman and who wouldn't?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Well, it was the municipal authorities or parties which put forward names, nominated individuals, and the Minister for Internal Affairs in Mostar made the ultimate decision as to appointments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the institutions that you enumerated, the police station and the police department, the Ministry for Internal Affairs and the government, of course, of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosnia, were the civilian organs of power and authority for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of what laws did you function in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: We worked according to the old laws of the Social Republic of Bosniz-Herzegovina, which we took over all the regulations and official gazettes for the area, the territory of Herceg-Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So apart from the formal changes that took place, are you saying that no criminal laws and criminal codes changed in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: That's right. We worked according to the codes that we took over when taking over the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If from this perspective today, you look back to 1992 and 1993 and you compare these years to the years before the war in Bosnia in 1989, 1990, 1991, you were a policeman during that time, and you are once again a policeman, and if you compare them to the present day, what would you say? Was there an increase in criminality in the war years compared to peacetime?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: The system functioned and the police was able to perform its duties, but then criminality in all its forms showed a marked increase. Today criminality is going down because the institutions are beginning to function again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, what were the causes of the increase in criminality in 1993, because those are the years that we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: One of the main causes of criminality was that the institutions of the system had broken down. The institutions were not able to function properly. There were no inspections, there were no courts of law functioning properly. Everything was in disarray and had ceased to function, and this was a breeding ground for crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether there were other causes. What about weapons and the population? How could a civilian, before the war, come by weapons of any kind and what happened during the war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, before the war there was set procedure, legal procedure which had to be followed in some -- if an individual wanted to carry weapons. He would have to have a certificate, he would have to have a medical certificate and his weapon had to be registered with the police force. But in 1992 and 1993, people began to arm themselves through various channels illegally, by underground means, and this was not a controlled process, and it took place en masse, because the war was imminent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, if somebody were to purchase weapons without the necessary certificates and permits, the police would take these -- confiscate these permits. Why in 1992 and 1993 did the police turn a blind eye to what was going on? It did not take away and confiscate the weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Because it was already a mass process, and the authorities could not come by the necessary weapons they needed and arm the people. So in a situation of that kind, the police could not confiscate weapons and it turned a blind eye to the fact that people were beginning to stock up on weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reason was the war, because people felt they needed to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. People would sell their cow to buy a rifle if they thought this was necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the authorities did not confiscate weapons. Does that mean the weapons were not confiscated either from the Croats or from the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We didn't take them away from Muslims or Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, what happened to the smuggling activities and illegal trading of arms, and how was this linked to the rise of crime?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Everything ceased to function. There were not -- we did not have the necessary consumer goods in our shops, so that smuggling became rampant. Goods were being bought and sold, people were making a lot of money buying goods cheaply and selling them at astronomical prices, and so they began to reap economic power, and crime was on the rise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these people who resorted to smuggling and reaped benefits from this, they were criminals, in fact, they had acted contrary to the law?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Yes. They had already armed themselves. They were criminals, individuals or groups, and they had weapons and they committed various crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a small police station did you have any aid and assistance with regard to professionals or in any other way from the central police authorities either from Sarajevo or Bosnia-Herzegovina, or from the police force in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: No. We had no professional help whatsoever. Quite simply, we were left to fend for ourselves as a police force. We had no material or professional assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the central authorities, did that function properly or did the municipality begin to act like a State within a State?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: The central authorities ceased to function. The system was disrupted. There were barriers. In Central Bosnia each municipality looked after itself and was a small State in its own right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is always a certain amount of civic discipline to a greater or lesser extent. How did the citizens, how did the inhabitants react when they found that their institutions were not functioning properly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: What happened was that the citizens themselves began to alter their conduct, and people who had never engaged in crime suddenly became criminals. They had weapons, and the circumstances that prevailed influenced people to change their behaviour and contact. They were frightened for their lives. They engaged in crime, looting and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at what the situation was like in the police force. At one point the police differentiated -- the Muslims left. Can you tell us how many Muslims left, how many Croats remained and what the reason for all this was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Well, the police split up at that moment when the Muslim policemen, together with their leadership, moved to the territory where the Muslims were the majority population. That was in Kacuni. At that time we were half, half, approximately, and 58 per cent of us, the Croats, remained in the police station in Busovaca, 50 per cent of the Muslims went to Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from that day on, in the territory of the municipality of Busovaca, there have been two police stations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There is a police station in Busovaca with Croats and a police station in Kacuni with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were halved as policemen in Busovaca. In addition to police work, are you in charge of some military matters?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Yes. Most of our work was channelled towards defence, and most of the policemen wanted to defend the frontlines and made themselves available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what about trained policemen and the technical equipment you needed and the financial resources you needed. What was the situation like in your police station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: The situation in the police station in Busovaca was very bad. There were only three or four of us who were trained policemen, who had completed the relevant schools, and the rest had no education related to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about vehicles, gasoline?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: We did not have any material resources. We had one vehicle, but we didn't have any gasoline for it, so we tried to make do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about expertise? For example, the institutes for studying blood traces and fingerprints, et cetera, did you have anything of that sort in the territory of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: No. All of these are small police stations, and even if such expertise, resources did exist, this was only in Zenica or in the Ministry in Sarajevo. We did not have a lab, and we didn't even have the simplest devices for taking fingerprints let alone anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have someone who could conduct a post-mortem and in this way help in terms of finding perpetrators of criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: No. We did not have a forensic expert of this nature. The only such expert was in Zenica, and he was not available to us then. This man still works as a forensic expert, and his services are still called upon, but he couldn't do a thing for us at that time. This is Mr. Turkic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was not accessible to you because of the war, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from this time distance and on the basis of your overall experience, if you analyse the crime that you explained to us that became rampant, how could you qualify it? Was it ethnically coloured, so to speak? Was it aimed against one national group only? Did the criminals come from one national group only? Could you tell us something more about that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, all criminal offences are against victims irrespective of ethnicity. Crimes were committed against Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you asserting that crime had its own logic of crime irrespective of interethnic relations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. According to its own law, it would have nothing to do with ethnicity. Victims were not specially selected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one time you introduced a curfew in Busovaca. Why was this done?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: A curfew was introduced in order to prevent crime and to control the movement of criminals, and for security and safety reasons in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, your police station introduced a certain procedure in respect of leaving Busovaca and coming back to Busovaca. Could you explain to the Court what this procedure was, if a citizen, irrespective of his ethnicity, wished to leave Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Any citizen who wanted to leave Busovaca would come to the police station and make statement to an authorised official stating the reasons why he wished to leave Busovaca, and then he was asked whether he was being mistreated by someone, whether he wants to leave the area of Busovaca of his own volition or for other reasons. Precisely with a view to preventing the mistreatment of citizens by individuals and groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best your recollection when and under what circumstances did the largest number of citizens of Muslim ethnicity leave Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Well, three or four days before the conflict broke out in January in 1993. Most of them, 90 per cent of the Muslim women and children left Busovaca and went to Zenica or to Kacuni to compact Muslim territories, so to speak, the majority of Muslim territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody expel them then or did they leave voluntarily? If they left voluntarily, what was the reason for that, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Nobody had made them do it. Only women and children left, and military-aged men stayed on in Busovaca. I think that they had received instructions from the Muslim leadership, which was not in Busovaca at all. They were already in Kacuni and they were instructed to remove their wives and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, why withdraw them three or four days before the war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Probably they were planning an attack, I don't know, probably for that reason. Because rumour had it that Busovaca would be attacked by the Mujahedin and the people from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this mass exodus from Busovaca, you say 90 per cent of the Muslim population had left before the Muslims attacked in January 1993. After that, were there any other big waves of departures of Muslims, or was it all on an individual basis mostly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: It was mostly on an individual basis, there were no more mass exoduses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we disregard these 90 per cent who left, these civilians who left before the war broke out in Busovaca, what was the reason for which part of these remaining 10 per cent left during these remaining few months, I mean, the first few months of 1993, why?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Well, part of them probably left out of fear, because they were afraid. Also, Croats came from other areas because they were afraid there, areas that were under Muslim control. And some left of their own initiative, just like that. People were probably afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say the people were afraid. Was this fear realistic? Was this well-founded fear? Did they have reasons for this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: No, they were equally protected, like all citizens in Busovaca, as regards the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that they had equal protection on the part of police, but was this protection sufficient? Was there violence and crime in spite of that directed against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Well, there were criminal acts that were committed against Muslims and the Croats, and within the scope of our responsibilities we took action, we tried to prevent this and we tried to protect people to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, could you please describe to the Court what the procedure was, for example, when your police station would receive a report saying that an explosive had gone off somewhere or, for example, a fire breaks out somewhere? What was the procedure involved when you received information of this kind?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Well, the usual professional procedure. In a police station this is a regular thing, and the officer on duty receives this information and then an investigation team is set up which goes and makes an inquest, and then a file is made and then operations take place in order to find the perpetrator. If an NN perpetrator, an unknown perpetrator is involved, there is, nevertheless, a file opened, and one always had the obligation to do something about this file and to find the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would also submit a report to the Prosecutor; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Yes, we would submit reports to the Prosecutor, both if the perpetrator was known or unknown, that was our duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, in your practice do you know of a single case that your police station received information on some violence, on a criminal act or something, and would not act if you heard that the victim was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: This did not happen. We always intervened the same way, regardless of whether this was a Muslim or a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, now we would like to distribute a set of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D443.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The last Defence Exhibit was 449, I thought, the map used by the last witness, 449.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, there was an error, the interpreter made a mistake, it was 442. That was the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well, we premarked this as 450. Could this be premarked as 450 and we will fill in 453 (sic) through 449 in the coming days, with the Court's permission?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All right, it could be 450 and use the other numbers later. No problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection? If that's going to make things easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have these for the translators, two groups, French and English. Mr. President, before we move on to this set, I would like to explain how this file has been organised. We have chapters that are marked with letters A through K. In chapter A, there are crimes against Muslims. Chapter B are documents that speak about criminal offences against Croats. In chapter C are, that is the police file related to damages to the mosque in Busovaca. In D are documents speaking of Muslims as perpetrators of criminal offences. In chapter E -- too fast? The next one is F, are statements of Muslims who are leaving Busovaca. G includes statements made by Croats who came to Busovaca. H are reports of the Busovaca police station. And I is information about Croats who fled to Busovaca from territories controlled by the BH army. In K are destroyed Croat houses in Busovaca on the territory under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And now, I'm going to -- also, every document in its Croatian version is marked with number 1 through 98, that is the last document. And in this way we wish to mark the area with a letter, and the numbers marked specific documents. Before we move on to these documents, I wish to ask our witness the following.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see all these documents and did you confirm to me that all these documents were written in the police station in Busovaca, except those related to J and K, referring to the houses that were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA
utterances.text: Yes, I saw these documents. These documents were signed by my colleagues and I know the text myself. Some of them I wrote myself, and the others I can recognise by the signatures and the institution involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are not going to go through all these documents, they speak for themselves, but we have one problem, and that is under H, we have reports of the police station in Busovaca. This summer we had these reports translated, but due to certain circumstances we did not obtain translations. So I suggest that we, nevertheless, use these reports, they are very important. We see these documents condensed in this report, so I would just like to read a few sentences from each report which I consider to be relevant. If you agree with this, all other documents are translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't know if there is an objection from the Prosecutor. Mr. Cayley? I know that is a lot of documents for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The whole file is a very large file, Mr. President, and the documents that my learned friend is referring to which he states have been translated are only provided in the Bosnian Croat language, so neither I nor my colleagues can actually read any of them. It will make cross-examination of the witness extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, excuse me. Perhaps I misinterpreted what Mr. Nobilo said. If I understood correctly, all the documents have been translated into English, at least, except for the documents from the binder H, for which there is neither French nor an English version. Did I interpret you correctly? Your difficulty, Mr. Cayley, stems from the fact that, first of all, it's a very large file, and in addition, in that file there are statements that are in Serbo-Croat. As regards the first point, Mr. Cayley, this is not the first time that one of the parties is faced with a big file. All right. Mr. Hayman is pulling out 456, I know, I know, I was sure you were going to pull that one out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With no witness, Mr. President. The Prosecutor produced no witness, no witness, when they tendered exhibits 406 and 456. So I don't -- well, I'm still listening to my learned friend, I'll put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, you see, I know you so well I can predict what you're going to say. Here I am with my colleagues in order to be sure that the conduct of the proceedings is just and equitable. This is not the first time that either of the parties has given many documents to the other party, and I'm sure that if there is a translation you will try to do as best you can. And if one day you have to, you need to bring the witness back, you can do so. But for the time being, I think it is the second question which causes some problem, that is, there are documents that are not translated either into French or English. Let me point out that the one who should complain the most is the presiding Judge, and I complain very rarely, I protest very rarely. I think we are going to do our best. As regards the Croatian documents, perhaps it would not be enough to read only a few lines, Mr. Nobilo. Perhaps that would not be sufficient. All right, we'll see. Perhaps you should read the document and we have a sight translation for it. Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: One last point, Mr. President. If we're going to go ahead with these documents and with this witness, then the Prosecutor would wish to reserve their right to call the witness back to be cross-examined on these documents when we have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I had suggested. Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think there is a distinction to be drawn, Mr. President.
